title: Sepsis to septic shock

objective: Early sepsis identification and sepsis management
secondaryObjectives: Shock states, including distributive and obstructive shock

Deliver early sepsis care: blood cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics ideally within the first hour in shock or probable sepsis (after a rapid assessment when sepsis is only possible), source control, crystalloid resuscitation and vasopressors to a mean arterial pressure target

sources.note: Septic shock: sepsis needing a vasopressor to hold MAP at 65 or more with lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid. Stated from the published definition; not re-opened this session.

brief.situation: Handover at 19:00. Bed 4, 58-year-old, 80 kg, admitted from the ED at 18:30 with fever, right flank pain and dysuria. The ED gave 1,000 mL of lactated Ringer's. A broad-spectrum antibiotic is ordered and on the unit; the first dose is not in yet, and blood cultures were not drawn in the ED. A sepsis order set is active.
handover: Temperature 39.1, HR 115, BP 92/50 (MAP 70) and drifting down, RR 24, SpO2 95% on 2 L.
A little confused about the date. ED lactate was not sent. Peripheral IVs: two, 18 gauge, both forearms.
Urine via Foley: about 30 mL in the last hour, dark.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Assessments examine the patient; orders and drips act. Some ask for a volume or dose.
Things take as long as they would on a unit: cultures take minutes to draw, a lactate comes back from the analyser, a bolus runs in, drips take minutes to work, the provider calls back.
While you wait on something you can skip ahead; the skip stops early at an alarm or a result.
Partway through you are asked to write what you think is happening. The case ends at the intensivist's review 2.5 hours in, then a debrief scores what you did.

then.log: Flushed and warm, a little confused about the date. Capillary refill 3 s. Breathing fast. Skin hot to the touch.
Warm peripheries but knees starting to mottle. Capillary refill 3-4 s. Drowsy but answers. Urine in the bag dark and scant.
Mottled knees, capillary refill over 4 s, cool fingers now. Drowsy, mumbling. Breathing fast and shallow.
Grey and mottled to the thighs, capillary refill over 5 s. Barely rousable. Weak thready pulse.
Crackles at both bases now, rising. Work of breathing up.

Drawing two sets of blood cultures from two sites (about 5 min).

whatNow.question: The picture is changing. What do you think is happening, and what are your next steps, in order?

parts.label: What is happening
parts.criteria: Names sepsis progressing to septic shock (or distributive shock from infection), supported by at least two of: falling MAP with tachycardia, lactate of 4 or more, mottling or slow capillary refill, confusion, falling urine output, fever with a urinary source.
parts.modelAnswer: Sepsis from a urinary source progressing to septic shock: falling MAP and rising heart rate, lactate above 4, mottled knees and slow capillary refill, confusion and little urine. The vessels are dilated and leaking, so fluid alone will not hold the pressure.

parts.label: What next
parts.criteria: Gives the first antibiotic now (cultures first only if they do not delay it), completes 30 mL/kg crystalloid and reassesses after each bolus, escalates to the provider for a norepinephrine order to a MAP of 65 or more (peripheral start acceptable), and plans a repeat lactate.
parts.modelAnswer: Blood cultures, then the antibiotic without delay; finish 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid and reassess after each bolus; call the provider with an SBAR naming septic shock and ask for norepinephrine to MAP 65 or more, started peripherally rather than waiting for a central line; look for the source; repeat the lactate in 2 hours.

source.cite: Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2026. Crit Care Med 2026;54(4) (published 2026-03-23); also Intensive Care Med 2026, doi:10.1007/s00134-026-08361-1
source.note: Septic shock: antimicrobials immediately, ideally within 1 h (as relayed).
Escalate within 15 min of the first MAP below 65.
Total time with MAP below 65 that still counts as a prompt restoration: 45 min. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

noProgress.rationale: Septic shock still below a MAP of 65 two and a half hours in is ongoing organ hypoperfusion, not a safe holding pattern, so this case calls it harm.

source.cite: Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2026. Crit Care Med 2026;54(4) (published 2026-03-23); also Intensive Care Med 2026, doi:10.1007/s00134-026-08361-1
source.note: MAP target about 65 (as relayed); persistent hypotension is the progressive harm the targets exist to prevent. The class choice is the author's, per docs/sims.md 9.2.

arrest.label: Cardiac arrest from refractory septic shock
arrest.narrative: The pressure kept falling until the heart stopped. PEA on the monitor: the code team is called. Septic shock that is not treated in time ends here.

stabilized.narrative: Two and a half hours in, MAP is holding at {map} on norepinephrine {neDose} mcg/kg/min, the antibiotic went in early after cultures, and the lactate is coming down. The ICU team takes over a patient who is getting better.

stabilizedLate.label: Stabilized, by a slower route
stabilizedLate.narrative: MAP is {map} at the 2.5-hour review and the patient is alive, but the route was slower or needed rescue: a late antibiotic, a late call, a long time below a MAP of 65, or a breathing tube for fluid overload.

time_up.label: Still in shock at the review
time_up.narrative: Two and a half hours in, MAP is still below 65. The kidneys and the brain have been underperfused for a long time.

expertPath.text: Look at the patient: warm, confused, fast breathing, MAP 70 and falling, HR 115. Probable sepsis with hypoperfusion: lactate now, cultures now.
Two sets of blood cultures (about 5 min), a lactate on the unit analyser, and the antibiotic hung the moment the cultures are drawn.
Start completing 30 mL/kg: the ED liter plus two 1,000 mL boluses of balanced crystalloid, reassessing after each.
Call the provider: septic shock from a urinary source, fluids not holding; ask for norepinephrine and the ICU team. Look for the source.
MAP sliding toward 65 with 30 mL/kg in: start norepinephrine peripherally at 0.1 (the provider has ordered it), titrate every 5 min to MAP 65 or more. Do not wait for a central line.
Repeat the lactate 2 hours after the first. Falling lactate, warmer skin and more urine say the resuscitation is working.

arrest.headline: Cardiac arrest from septic shock
arrest.body: The most useful kind of run to learn from. Look at the first hour: when the antibiotic went in, when the provider was called, and when the MAP first dropped below 65 with nothing to hold it.

stabilized.headline: Stabilized: septic shock treated on time
stabilized.body: Cultures, then the antibiotic within the hour, 30 mL/kg with reassessment, an early call and a peripheral norepinephrine start. That is the expert path.

stabilizedLate.headline: Stabilized, by a slower route
stabilizedLate.body: The patient made it, but something cost time or needed rescue. Check the antibiotic time, the call, the minutes below a MAP of 65 and the total fluid.

time_up.headline: Still in shock at the review
time_up.body: The pressure never came back to 65. The usual cause is a late antibiotic, a vasopressor started late or too low, or waiting for a central line.

scoring.modelReasoning: Sepsis from a urinary source is progressing to septic shock: falling MAP with a rising heart rate, lactate above 4, mottling and slow capillary refill, confusion and falling urine output. Antimicrobials are time-critical in septic shock (immediately, ideally within an hour); blood cultures come first only when drawing them does not delay the dose. At least 30 mL/kg of crystalloid is given for hypoperfusion and reassessed after each bolus, because the leak means more fluid is not always better. When MAP stays below 65 despite fluid, norepinephrine is first line and can start through a good peripheral line rather than waiting for central access. Escalate early with a clear SBAR, look for a source that may need draining, and trend the lactate.

culturesFirst.ask: Cultures are being drawn now. If drawing them were going to take another 45 minutes, should the antibiotic wait for them?

choices.label: No: give the antibiotic, cultures as soon as possible

culturesFirst.explain: No. Cultures before antibiotics matters because a dose can sterilize the blood and hide the organism, but in septic shock the antibiotic is time-critical. The guidelines put cultures first only when drawing them causes no substantial delay.

source.cite: Levy MM, Evans LE, Rhodes A. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign Bundle: 2018 update. Crit Care Med 2018;46(6):997-1000 (the Hour-1 bundle)
source.note: Hour-1 bundle as listed by WikEM: obtain blood cultures before antibiotics, but do not delay antibiotics to obtain cultures. SSC 2021 gives the 1-hour target in possible septic shock.

bolusEffect.ask: This bolus will lift the MAP while it runs in. What do you expect over the next hour after it finishes?
bolusEffect.explain: It drifts back down. In septic shock the vessels are dilated and leaky, so much of a bolus leaves the circulation within the hour. That is why each bolus is followed by a reassessment, and why a vasopressor follows when fluid does not hold the pressure.

source.cite: Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2026. Crit Care Med 2026;54(4) (published 2026-03-23); also Intensive Care Med 2026, doi:10.1007/s00134-026-08361-1
source.note: FLAG: the guideline recommends reassessing with dynamic measures (Rec 49, as relayed) and starting a vasopressor for hypotension during or after fluid; the 'drifts back within the hour' time course is this scenario's own teaching model (leakTau 60 min), not a number from the guideline.

peripheral.ask: MAP 61 after 30 mL/kg. The provider is about to call back. No central line yet. What do you plan to suggest?

choices.label: Start norepinephrine now through a good peripheral IV
Wait for a central line before any vasopressor

peripheral.explain: Start it peripherally. The 2021 guideline suggests starting a vasopressor peripherally rather than delaying until central access, and the 2026 algorithm (as relayed) says the same. Use a large proximal vein and check the site often; move it to a central line when one is in.

source.cite: Evans L, Rhodes A, Alhazzani W, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2021. Crit Care Med 2021;49(11):e1063-e1143. doi:10.1097/CCM.0000000000005337
source.note: SSC 2021: suggest starting vasopressors peripherally rather than delaying until central venous access (weak). SSC 2026 algorithm figure, as relayed by a secondary summary: start peripherally if no central access.

lactateTrend.ask: If this repeat lactate comes back lower than the first, is the resuscitation finished?

choices.label: Not on its own: check MAP, perfusion and urine too

lactateTrend.explain: Not on its own. A falling lactate is a good sign and the guidelines use serial lactate to guide resuscitation, with capillary refill time as an adjunct. Read it beside the MAP, the skin, the mentation and the urine output.

source.cite: Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2026. Crit Care Med 2026;54(4) (published 2026-03-23); also Intensive Care Med 2026, doi:10.1007/s00134-026-08361-1
source.note: Rec 51 (serial lactate to guide resuscitation) and Rec 52 (capillary refill time as an adjunct), as relayed by a secondary summary (clinical-database.com, Part 3).
